title: Two-qubit cryo-CMOS control of a spin register in diamond
authors: H. B. van Ommen, N. E. Fakkel, M. van Riggelen, J. Yun, L. A. Enthoven, M. A. B. ElBadry, F. Sebastiano, M. Babaie, T. H. Taminiau
abstract: Utility-scale quantum technologies will not only require a well-performing quantum platform, but also classical control hardware that is scalable, efficient, and meets the design requirements set by the quantum system of interest. One approach is the application of silicon CMOS technology, a highly scalable and mature technology, to design application-specific integrated circuits (ASIC) that are optimized for the quantum system. In this work, we present two-qubit control of electron and nuclear spins in NV centres in diamond, using a cryogenic CMOS qubit controller integrated with a diamond quantum device in a cryostat. Using Gate Set Tomography (GST) we characterize the performance of the single-qubit gates on both electron- and carbon nuclear spins, and analyze the limiting noise processes. We use dynamical decoupling to engineer a two-qubit gate, and estimate $F_\text{2q,avg} = 95(2)\%$ for the electron-nuclear two-qubit gate fidelity. Our demonstration of cryo-CMOS-driven two-qubit gates is a key step towards highly-integrated quantum devices based on colour centres.
summary: This paper presents a breakthrough in quantum hardware integration by demonstrating two-qubit gate operations on diamond spin qubits using a custom cryo-CMOS controller. By integrating the classical control electronics directly with the quantum chip at cryogenic temperatures, the authors achieve high gate fidelities, marking a significant step toward scalable, practical quantum processors.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is developing scalable, efficient, and integrated classical control hardware necessary for utility-scale quantum technologies.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated two-qubit gates on electron and nuclear spins in diamond using a cryo-CMOS controller, achieving an estimated two-qubit gate fidelity of 95(2)%.
method: The work involves integrating a custom cryo-CMOS ASIC with a diamond quantum device in a cryostat to perform precise pulse control, characterized using Gate Set Tomography (GST).
model_or_system: The physical system is a solid-state quantum register utilizing electron and nearby carbon nuclear spins within Nitrogen-Vacancy (NV) centers in diamond. Control is achieved via a cryo-CMOS controller generating both GHz (electron) and MHz (nuclear) pulses.
key_observables: Two-qubit gate fidelity ($F_{2q,avg}$), Rabi frequencies ($\Omega_e, \Omega_{c0}, \Omega_{c1}$), and coherence times ($T_2$).
important_parameters: Operating temperature ($\approx 6$ K), electron spin frequency ($f_e \approx 2.6 	ext{ GHz}$), and nuclear spin frequencies ($	ext{MHz}$ range).
main_assumptions: The core gate operations are performed cryogenically, though initialization and readout still require external room-temperature control. Heat generation from the CMOS chip is noted as a potential limitation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the integrated setup in a cryostat, the detailed architecture of the CMOS controller (showing GHz and MHz paths), and measurements demonstrating coherence time scaling and gate fidelity characterization.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for integrated control hardware to detailing the cryo-CMOS architecture, demonstrating single- and two-qubit gate operations, and concluding with the fidelity results for the integrated system.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles the critical engineering bottleneck—the classical control electronics—for solid-state quantum computing platforms, which is a major focus area for quantum information scientists.

The cryo-CMOS qubit controller chip [23] and diamond qubit device hosting NV centres are placed together on a printed circuit board in a cryostat at 6 K. Solid Immer- sion Lenses are used to improve the optical collection efficiency of the NV centre emission. The CMOS chip autonomously performs a quantum circuit on the qubits. Qubit initialization and readout are performed by the room-temperature control system. Prior to cir- cuit runtime the CMOS chip is programmed to perform the desired quantum circuit(s).
